title: The Truthfulness of the Word
english: The Word is not obscure, but rather simple and true; it fully embodies the statement: 'Our Word, who is with you, did not become yes and no.'

That is to say, He does not contend with Himself or suffer from the sickness of the incompatible, sometimes praising a thing and sometimes reproving it, but rather remains truthful in His proclamation.
God is therefore faithful, meaning He is both without falsehood and entirely true.
The rhetoricians of the Greeks will glorify the gods they have traditionally assumed in various ways, saying both yes and no.
For truth is not found among them, but rather falsehood.
Consequently, they are shaken by diverse opinions.
But how could the true Son, who is by nature the Son of the God of all power, become yes and no? ....
Likewise, the Son who is by nature from Him, who was proclaimed in you through us by me, Silvanus, and Timothy, did not become yes and no.
For every true word concerning Him has come to pass through the voice of the diviners.
And all the promises of God that He speaks are 'yes' in Him; indeed, we have received through Him every zeal and every promise from God and the Father.
And this is in the Temple, that is, in truth.
For these things have reached their fulfillment through Christ.
For 'death was swallowed up in victory' (1 Cor 15:54), the power of corruption has been shattered, the unyielding shall cease, and with them, dishonor.
This is just as the most wise Paul also said in his earlier epistle.
Furthermore, we have been shown to be both heirs and partakers of that very kingdom of the saints.

For he himself will speak to us from the divine throne, in whom the 'yes' resides: 'Come, you blessed of the Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world' (Matt 25:34). Indeed, we are servants according to our nature.
But through him we were called from slavery to freedom, from corruption to incorruption, and we were delivered from the bondage of the devil.
Every promise of God, therefore, through Christ alone, carries the 'yes'.
But the 'no' is altogether unacceptable.
Which is the denial.
For he himself is the truth.
He also demonstrates this decisively: that God is, according to nature.

For if he would not lie regarding the promises, but rather fulfills them for the saints—even though he is the one distributing the good things of God the Father—how could he not be truly and by nature the Son, and as God from God, in whom 'every good gift and every perfect gift' (James 1:17) is not spoken falsely? That the Word is truthful, he points to by saying, 'Therefore also through him to God the Amen for our glory.'
Since he himself is the Mediator, through whom alone the Father is approachable, and in whom is every spiritual gift, through him indeed everything shall be the end of prayer.
And this is the Amen.
Furthermore, the Son himself has instructed us toward this, saying to the holy apostles, 'And in that day you will not ask me' (John 16:23) anything.
'Amen, amen I say to you, if you ask anything of the Father, he will give it to you in my name' (John 16:24).
'Until now you have asked nothing in my name' (John 16:24).
'Ask and you shall receive, so that your joy may be filled' (John 16:24). Through him, therefore, is the Amen to God the Father for our glory.
For it is our custom to bring every prayer to a close in the name of Christ.

Since he himself would not be thought to be fitting to be glorified, we see clearly through the blessed prophet Jacob, who says, 'Judah, your brothers have praised you' (Gen 49:8); for Christ came from the tribe of Judah according to the flesh. As for the fullness of the prophet Isaiah, he says, 'I saw the Lord of Sabaoth sitting upon a high and exalted throne' (Isa 6:1), surrounded by the seraphim, who stand around him calling him holy and naming him Lord of Sabaoth, declaring that the heaven and the earth are full of his glory. Because he has beheld him, the Son, the wise John says, proving this: 'These things Isaiah said, that he saw the glory...'
translator_notes: p7 contains a trailing ellipsis in the Greek (....) indicating a gap in the text.
The Greek text ends mid-sentence in paragraph 4: 'εἶδεν τὴν δόξαν' (saw the glory...).
Paragraph 2 contains a slight grammatical tension in 'ἀμοιρήσειεν' (optative) which I have rendered as a conditional/concessive thought.

title: The Divinity and Humanity of Christ
english: …Him also and he spoke about him. Surely the Father is glorified through Him; and since He has been established as a 'propitiation through faith,' He has also become a 'minister of the saints' by virtue of His humanity, performing the prayer of each saint as a spiritual sacrifice.
For through Him is our 'Amen.'
One cannot think otherwise than that it is necessary both to worship Him and to glorify Him together with the One who was born from among us and with the heavenly multitude of the holy spirits.

For Paul the Lawgiver once said, 'When He shall again bring the firstborn into the inhabited world,' saying, 'And let all angels worship Him' of God. To whom among existing things is it obscure that He is the Only-begotten, according to the conception of God? For He is born alone from the Only-begotten of the Father.
And since each of us has become a brother to many in the midst of us, He has been established as the Firstborn.
Furthermore, in addition to being the Only-begotten as God, He has also been employed as the Firstborn because of His humanity.
And the one who confirms us with you into Christ, etc.

God and Father confirms us into Christ, having strengthened a right and unshakeable faith in the souls of all, persuading them to believe that He is God by nature and in truth, even if He was seen among us in form, the One above all creation having been born according to the flesh from a woman.

Indeed, our Lord Jesus Christ himself reflected the confession of Peter, who was clearly declaring, 'You are the Christ, the Son of the living God' (Matt 16:16). The Lord echoed him, saying, 'Blessed are you, Simon, son of Jonah, for flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father who is in the heavens' (Matt 16:17). Since you have been brought into the experience of this mystery, it is fitting that it serves as a kind of initiation from above and from the Father.
For He himself confirms us into Christ, the one who has sealed us, anointed us as God, and given us the pledge of the Spirit.

It would not be inconsistent for us, because of these things, that the Son had not become a 'yes and no' (2 Cor 1:20). Rather, He is the true God, and in Him is the 'yes' for all good things. Because it is said that God seals us, anoints us, and gives us the pledge of the Spirit, Christ is the one fulfilling these things in us; He does so not as a subordinate, nor as an alien anointing and sealing us with the Spirit, but by His own self and by that of the Father.
In both is the Holy Spirit, through the identity of essence, not divided, but as proceeding from the Father through the Son upon the creation.
For He breathed into the holy apostles, saying, 'Receive the Holy Spirit' (John 20:22). Through Him and in Him, we have been sealed with the divine and the intelligible, according to the likeness.

For the divine apostle, writing to the Galatians, said, 'My children, whom I suffer pains for again, until Christ is formed in you' (Gal 4:19). If we are being formed into Christ, thereby enriching ourselves with the divine likeness, then He Himself is the image of God and the Father and the precise representation; this is not merely as we have been called toward a similarity through participation in sanctification, but rather by nature and essentially.
For He who is God by nature, truly God toward nature and from His own being, would possess nothing alien.
And He also was sealed by God and the Father, as the most wise John says.

For 'He who received His testimony sealed [it], saying that God is true' (1 John 5:6). Yet He was sealed again, not in the same manner as we are, but rather He Himself is entirely signified once in the nature of the Son, as the Father is being described essentially.

He affirmed this by saying, 'He who has seen me has seen the Father' (John 14:9). Thanks be to God, who always triumphs in us through Christ and makes the fragrance of His knowledge manifest in every place.
The apostles give thanks…

title: Christ as the Fragrance of the Knowledge of God
english: …Being tested and suffering, they boast in the contests fought for the sake of Christ.

For just as Christ has been triumphed for our sake, having endured the death on the wood and having been perfected through sufferings, so they claim they shall be triumphed for his sake, that is, to be known everywhere and to shine through trials and to conquer the world; for this reason, they are ready to suffer all things with great joy for the sake of the name of Christ.
For they are partakers of his sufferings, as it is said, partakers of the glory that is about to be revealed (Romans 8:17).

They say that God is the one triumphing in them, not as one who causes them to suffer nor indeed as one who heaps up tribulations upon them, but rather that, according to what seems to them, those proclaiming Jesus throughout all under heaven (Acts 2:36) fall into trials for his sake.
For without trials to be approved is impossible.
The fruit of these is that they suffer in Christ—that is, through Christ—which is a glorious thing and a medium of good hopes.

What, then, is this fragrance of the knowledge of God and Father, which is made manifest to the world through the holy apostles in every place? As they themselves declare, the law-giving Paul will teach this again, saying, 'For we do not preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord, and ourselves as your slaves through Jesus Christ' (2 Corinthians 4:5). And again, 'For I determined to know nothing among you except Christ Jesus and him being crucified' (1 Corinthians 2:2).

Furthermore, in what manner shall he who was born of a woman, having endured the cross and having submitted to death, even if he rose alive again, be a fragrance of the knowledge of the God and Father? If, as some suppose, Christ is perceived by us as a mere god-bearing man, and not as God existing by nature—even if it were perceived that the Word from God, having foreseen the human condition, acted economically—it would not follow that His nature toward us, and beyond nothingness, would have been fragrant of the God and Father. Nor would a fragrance have come from one who does not know death, even as death draws from it.

How then is the Christ the fragrance of the knowledge of the Father? It is evident, is it not, that he is understood and is God, even if he appeared in the flesh among us. For in what way do those proclaiming Christ announce to the world that he is God by nature and in truth? Otherwise, how could they perceive Jesus? Furthermore, in what way do the holy mystagogues say that God and Father reconciles the world to himself in Christ, unless one had perceived the Word proceeding from God toward union with the human, as this is required by the wise economy?

For the divinely appointed disciples announce, speaking in spirit, not as if the Word of God had merely dwelt in a man, but as having become flesh—that is, having become united to flesh possessing a rational soul; for in this way he would also be the lord of the fragrance of the crucified.

Thus, even if he were perceived in the flesh—or even if he were not, but remained as if he had not yet come among us—the Word from God is the fragrance of the knowledge of God and the Father, as the one who, in his own nature, sends forth fragrance toward us.

And if what I say is true, how could he be a generated being and be numbered among those who receive generation from those who do not exist? For he could not become a fragrance of the uncreated, nor a generated thing of the non-existent.
For we do not see the generated in the ungenerated, nor the ungenerated in the generated.
But the Son truly showed the Father within himself; therefore, he is God according to nature because of the identity of essence.
Let the Son also be heard toward us: 'Your name is a fragrance emptied out'; for through him and in him, we have known the Father and God from whom he is begotten.
That of Christ we are a fragrance to God among those being saved and among those being destroyed.
